title: What happens if my R&D tax credit is denied?
description: If the IRS denies a federal R&D tax credit, the business must repay the disallowed credit plus interest and a 20% penalty unless reasonable cause exists.
summary: If the IRS denies a business's federal R&D tax credit under IRC Section 41, it must repay 100% of the disallowed credit or forfeit a frozen refund, plus compounding interest from the unextended return due date and a 20% penalty under IRC § 6676 or § 6662 unless reasonable cause exists. Audit defense costs and multi-year examinations add exposure.

body.text: If the IRS denies a business's federal R&D tax credit under IRC Section 41, it must repay 100% of the disallowed credit or forfeit a frozen refund, plus compounding interest from the unextended return due date and a 20% penalty under IRC § 6676 or § 6662 unless reasonable cause exists. Audit defense costs and multi-year examinations add exposure.

When the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) denies a corporate Research and Development (R&D) tax credit claim under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41 (26 U.S.C. § 41), the disallowance immediately converts an anticipated tax asset into a compounding financial, statutory, and operational liability. Depending on whether the claimed credit has already reduced tax paid or is awaiting refund disbursement, the claimant faces either a 100% recapture of the disallowed tax benefit as an underpayment of tax under 26 U.S.C. § 6664(a)—accruing compounding statutory interest from the original unextended return due date under 26 U.S.C. § 6601(a) and (b)(1)—or an immediate administrative rejection and freeze of the requested refund. In addition to principal loss and statutory interest, the taxpayer faces a 20% civil penalty on the disallowed "excessive amount" of an erroneous claim for refund or credit under 26 U.S.C. § 6676(a) or a 20% accuracy-related penalty on a resulting tax underpayment attributable to negligence or substantial understatement of income tax under 26 U.S.C. § 6662(a) and (b)(1)–(2), unless the taxpayer establishes reasonable cause and good faith under the governing statutory standards.

Beyond direct tax deficiency and penalty assessments, defending a challenged or denied R&D tax credit claim imposes substantial operational drag across the enterprise. Because the taxpayer bears the entire legal burden of establishing that each discrete business component satisfies all four statutory tests under IRC § 41(d)(1) and Treasury Regulation (26 CFR) § 1.41-4(a)(2), audit defense and administrative appeals require retrospectively compiling contemporaneous engineering records, project-level accounting ledgers, and employee testimony across organizational tiers. Furthermore, an initial credit denial flags methodological and recordkeeping deficiencies that frequently trigger multi-year IRS examinations across open prior and subsequent tax filings.
I. Executive Synthesis: Immediate Statutory and Operational Consequences of R&D Tax Credit Denial

Within the compliance framework governing federal research credits, the disallowance of an R&D tax credit claim is not merely a forfeited tax incentive; it initiates a cascading financial and administrative liability across tax principal, statutory additions to tax, and examination defense costs. Under federal tax law in force as of November 2026, a denied R&D credit triggers three primary statutory and operational consequences:

items: Principal Recapture or Refund Disallowance and Statutory Interest (26 U.S.C. §§ 6601, 6664): If an R&D tax credit was claimed on an original return to offset income tax liability or was already disbursed as a tax refund, its subsequent disallowance creates an "underpayment" under 26 U.S.C. § 6664(a), requiring the taxpayer to repay 100% of the disallowed credit amount. Under 26 U.S.C. § 6601(a) and (b)(1), interest on that underpayment accrues at the federal underpayment rate established under IRC § 6621 from the "last date prescribed for payment"—which is the unextended original due date of the tax return for that taxable year, determined without regard to any filing extension or the later filing date of an amended return—until the date the tax is paid.

Statutory Penalty Regimes (26 U.S.C. §§ 6676, 6662, 6663): Under 26 U.S.C. § 6676(a) and (b), the IRS is authorized to assess a 20% civil penalty on the "excessive amount" (the disallowed portion) of an erroneous claim for credit or refund, a provision significantly strengthened by Section 209 of the Protecting Americans from Tax Hikes (PATH) Act of 2015 (Pub. L. 114-113) when Congress replaced the former "reasonable basis" exception with a stricter "reasonable cause" standard. Where the disallowance results in a tax underpayment, 26 U.S.C. § 6662(a) and (b)(1)–(2) impose a 20% accuracy-related penalty for negligence or disregard of rules or regulations, or for a substantial understatement of income tax. Under the statutory coordination rule in 26 U.S.C. § 6676(d), the 20% penalty under IRC § 6676 and the 20% penalty under IRC § 6662 do not stack on the same dollar of disallowed credit; rather, IRC § 6676 applies where no underpayment penalty is imposed (such as when an erroneous refund claim is intercepted and frozen prior to disbursement), whereas IRC § 6662 applies when an underpayment arises. Moreover, under Industry Director Directive #2 (IDD No. 2), IRS revenue agents disallowing a research credit refund are required to evaluate penalties such as IRC § 6676 and obtain concurrence from an R&D technical adviser before waiving them.

Substantiation Burden and Judicial Disallowance Standards (26 U.S.C. § 41(d); 26 CFR § 1.41-4): Federal courts strictly enforce the component-by-component evidentiary requirements of IRC § 41. In Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-15, aff'd, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), and Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113 (Dec. 23, 2024), the courts denied 100% of the examined R&D credits because the taxpayers lacked contemporaneous, activity-level documentation establishing that specific technological uncertainty existed at the outset of each project and that at least 80% ("substantially all") of the research activities per business component constituted elements of a structured Process of Experimentation (POE).

body.text: These legal realities demonstrate that reactive audit defense after filing an aggressive or poorly documented R&D claim carries a low probability of success and substantial financial exposure.
II. Financial and Statutory Liability Following R&D Tax Credit Disallowance

When an R&D tax credit claim is disallowed by the IRS, the resulting financial burden spans direct principal clawback, compounding statutory underpayment interest, civil tax penalties, and professional audit defense expenditures.
2.1 Direct Financial Recapture and Underpayment Interest Under IRC Section 6601

When an R&D credit that has already been utilized to reduce federal income tax liability (or refunded in cash to the taxpayer) is subsequently denied upon IRS examination, the disallowance creates an underpayment under 26 U.S.C. § 6664(a), obligating the taxpayer to repay 100% of the disallowed credit principal. Under 26 U.S.C. § 6664(a), an "underpayment" is defined as the amount by which the tax imposed by Title 26 exceeds the excess of the sum of the amount shown as the tax by the taxpayer on the return plus amounts previously assessed or collected without assessment, over the amount of rebates made. Because corporate claimants frequently budget for and deploy R&D credit cash savings into ongoing capital expenditures, hiring, or research operations upon receipt, a retrospective disallowance years later creates an acute working-capital reversal that may force short-term borrowing or the reallocation of operational funds.

In addition to principal repayment, the taxpayer owes statutory interest under 26 U.S.C. § 6601 (in force through Pub. L. 119-134, updated October 20, 2026). Under 26 U.S.C. § 6601(a) and (b)(1) and 26 CFR § 301.6601-1, if any amount of tax imposed by Title 26 is not paid on or before the "last date prescribed for payment," interest on that unpaid amount at the underpayment rate established under IRC § 6621 accrues for the period from such "last date prescribed for payment" until the date paid.

Specifically, 26 U.S.C. § 6601(b)(1) mandates that the last date prescribed for payment of the tax shall be determined under Chapter 62 (specifically 26 U.S.C. § 6151(a)) "without regard to any extension of time for payment or any installment agreement entered into under section 6159". Consequently, the statutory interest clock starts on the unextended original due date of the tax return for that taxable year, rather than the actual filing date of an extended return or a subsequent amended return. If a corporate taxpayer obtained a six-month filing extension or claimed the R&D credit via an amended return (Form 1120-X) filed years later, underpayment interest on a recaptured tax reduction runs from the unextended original return due date (or, where an excessive refund was actually paid out in cash, interest on the erroneous refund runs from the date of the payment under IRC § 6602). Under 26 U.S.C. § 6601(e)(1), interest prescribed under Section 6601 is treated as tax: it must be paid upon notice and demand and is assessed, collected, and paid in the same manner as taxes. Furthermore, under 26 U.S.C. § 6601(e)(2)(B), interest on an accuracy-related penalty or fraud penalty imposed under Part II of Subchapter A of Chapter 68 (IRC §§ 6662, 6662A, or 6663) accrues from the date on which the return of the tax is required to be filed (including any extensions) until the date of payment of the addition to tax, whereas interest on other assessable penalties under 26 U.S.C. § 6601(e)(2)(A) begins running if not paid within 21 calendar days from the date of notice and demand (or 10 business days if the amount equals or exceeds $100,000). Because IRS examinations and U.S. Tax Court litigation routinely span multiple years, compounding statutory interest adds substantially to the final cash liability.

Verification against the underlying source (Fierce Healthcare, November 20, 2025, reporting MDaudit healthcare vendor benchmark data from the first three quarters of 2025 across more than 1.2 million providers and 4,500 facilities) confirms the statistic within its original sector: across hospital inpatient and outpatient settings, the average denied dollar amount for a Medicare Advantage medical billing claim rose 22.4% in 2025 to approximately $1,000. The same MDaudit dataset recorded a 30% year-over-year increase per customer in total at-risk amounts for external healthcare payer audits (with per-claim audit request amounts rising 18%, averaging $17,000 per request in hospital settings and $1,172 in professional medical settings, and commercial payers accounting for 45% of total at-risk amounts versus 28% for Medicare and Medicaid). While the 22.4% figure is verified within the healthcare revenue-cycle sector, it measures hospital medical insurance claim reimbursements rather than IRS tax credit disallowances; no primary IRS dataset measures an equivalent year-over-year percentage change in average disallowed R&D tax credit dollar amounts.
2.2 Statutory Penalties: Erroneous Claim (IRC Section 6676), Accuracy-Related (IRC Section 6662), and Fraud (IRC Section 6663)
The Internal Revenue Code enforces compliance in tax credit filings through distinct, non-overlapping civil penalty provisions codified in Chapter 68 of Title 26.
1. The 20% Erroneous Claim for Refund or Credit Penalty (26 U.S.C. § 6676)

Under 26 U.S.C. § 6676(a) (originally added by Pub. L. 110-28, Title VIII, § 8247(a), May 25, 2007, 121 Stat. 204, and in force through Pub. L. 119-138, updated November 3, 2026), if a claim for refund or credit with respect to income or employment tax is made for an "excessive amount," the person making such claim is liable for a civil penalty in an amount equal to 20 percent of the excessive amount, unless it is shown that the claim for such excessive amount is due to reasonable cause. Under 26 U.S.C. § 6676(b), the term "excessive amount" means, in the case of any person, the amount by which the amount of the claim for refund or credit for any taxable year exceeds the amount of such claim allowable under Title 26 for such taxable year—that is, the disallowed portion of the claimed credit. Under 26 U.S.C. § 6676(c) (added by Pub. L. 111-152, § 1409(d), Mar. 30, 2010, and amended by Pub. L. 114-113 and Pub. L. 115-141), any excessive amount attributable to a transaction lacking economic substance within the meaning of IRC § 6662(b)(6) (and IRC § 7701(o)) is barred from being treated as due to reasonable cause.

As documented in the IRS Practice Unit Erroneous Claim for Refund or Credit Penalty (Document Control Number PEN-P-006, updated February 25, 2022) and the statutory amendment notes to 26 U.S.C. § 6676, the penalty may be asserted against taxpayers filing an original return, an amended return (such as Form 1040-X, Amended U.S. Individual Income Tax Return, or Form 1120-X, Amended U.S. Corporation Income Tax Return), Form 843 (Claim for Refund and Request for Abatement), or informal/protective claims and affirmative examination issues contending an overpayment of tax, provided at least a portion of the claimed refund is frozen and unpaid prior to disbursement. The IRS generally applies a three-year limitation period running from the date the claim for refund or credit was filed, using Form 872-EC to extend the assessment period for IRC § 6676 penalties specifically and Form 8278 (or Form 3870 in joint-return cases) to compute and assess the penalty under non-deficiency procedures.

In the Protecting Americans from Tax Hikes (PATH) Act of 2015 (Pub. L. 114-113, Div. Q, Title II, § 209(b)–(c), enacted December 18, 2015, 129 Stat. 3084–3085), Congress strengthened IRC § 6676 in three ways for claims filed on or after December 18, 2015:

items: Elevation of Relief Standard: Congress amended 26 U.S.C. § 6676(a) and (c) by substituting "is due to reasonable cause" for "has a reasonable basis". For claims filed before December 18, 2015, a taxpayer could avoid the penalty by showing a lower "reasonable basis" (under Treas. Reg. § 1.6662-3(b)(3) and § 1.6662-4(d)(3)(iii)). For claims filed on or after December 18, 2015, the taxpayer must satisfy the stricter subjective standard of "reasonable cause" (under Treas. Reg. § 1.6664-4), which evaluates whether the taxpayer exercised ordinary business care and prudence based on all pertinent facts and circumstances, including the taxpayer's knowledge and sophistication, the complexity of the tax issue, and the nature of the claimed benefit. Claims lacking a factual basis, unsubstantiated claims, or claims unsupported by adequate books and records fail this standard.
Elimination of Earned Income Credit Exemption: Pub. L. 114-113, § 209(b), struck out the prior parenthetical exemption for claims relating to the Earned Income Credit (EIC) under IRC § 32.

Revision of Underpayment Definition: The PATH Act amended the definition of "underpayment" in 26 U.S.C. § 6664(a) so that refundable credits can reduce the amount of "tax shown on the return" below zero when calculating an underpayment, statutorily reversing Rand v. Commissioner, 141 T.C. 376 (2013).

body.text: Additionally, effective for claims for credit or refund filed after July 4, 2025, Public Law 119-21 (Title VII, § 70605(f), July 4, 2025, 139 Stat. 288) expanded 26 U.S.C. § 6676(a) by substituting "income or employment tax" for "income tax" (superseding the pre-2025 limitation noted in the 2022 IRS Practice Unit that § 6676 applied solely to income taxes and not employment taxes).
2. The 20% Accuracy-Related Penalty on Underpayments (26 U.S.C. § 6662)

When the disallowance of an R&D tax credit results in an underpayment of tax required to be shown on a return (for example, where the credit reduced tax paid on an original return or where an erroneous refund was already disbursed to the taxpayer), 26 U.S.C. § 6662(a) (in force through Pub. L. 119-120, updated October 7, 2026) adds to the tax an amount equal to 20 percent of the portion of the underpayment to which Section 6662 applies. Under 26 U.S.C. § 6664(b), accuracy-related penalties apply only in cases where a tax return is filed (other than a substitute return prepared by the Secretary under IRC § 6020(b)).

In the context of R&D tax credit denials, two primary triggers under 26 U.S.C. § 6662(b) apply. The first trigger is negligence or disregard of rules or regulations under 26 U.S.C. § 6662(b)(1) and (c), where "negligence" includes any failure to make a reasonable attempt to comply with the provisions of Title 26 (such as failing to verify the factual accuracy of a credit claim or failing to maintain required substantiation under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(d) and § 1.6001-1), and "disregard" includes any careless, reckless, or intentional disregard of tax rules or regulations. The second trigger is a substantial understatement of income tax under 26 U.S.C. § 6662(b)(2) and (d), where an "understatement" under 26 U.S.C. § 6662(d)(2)(A) means the excess of the amount of tax required to be shown on the return for the taxable year over the amount of tax imposed which is shown on the return, reduced by any rebate within the meaning of IRC § 6211(b)(2). For corporations (other than an S corporation or a personal holding company as defined in IRC § 542), a substantial understatement of income tax exists for any taxable year under 26 U.S.C. § 6662(d)(1)(B) if the amount of the understatement exceeds the lesser of 10 percent of the tax required to be shown on the return for the taxable year (or, if greater, $10,000), or $10,000,000. For individual taxpayers (such as shareholders or partners claiming flow-through R&D credits from S corporations or partnerships), a substantial understatement exists under 26 U.S.C. § 6662(d)(1)(A) and (C) if the understatement exceeds the greater of 10 percent of the tax required to be shown on the return for the taxable year (substituted with "5 percent" under § 6662(d)(1)(C) if the taxpayer claims any Qualified Business Income deduction allowed under IRC § 199A for the taxable year) or $5,000.
3. Statutory Coordination, Penalty Exceptions, and Corrections to Penalty Claims

Under 26 U.S.C. § 6676(d) (Coordination with other penalties), Section 6676 "shall not apply to any portion of the excessive amount of a claim for refund or credit which is subject to a penalty imposed under part II of subchapter A of chapter 68" (namely, IRC § 6662 accuracy-related penalties on underpayments, IRC § 6662A accuracy-related penalties on reportable transaction understatements, or IRC § 6663 fraud penalties). Likewise, 26 U.S.C. § 6662(b) explicitly provides that Section 6662 "shall not apply to any portion of an underpayment on which a penalty is imposed under section 6663". Specifically, if an erroneous refund claim is intercepted and frozen before being paid out, no underpayment exists and the 20% IRC § 6676 penalty applies; conversely, if the credit has already reduced tax paid or been refunded, an underpayment arises and the 20% IRC § 6662 accuracy-related penalty (or 75% IRC § 6663 fraud penalty) applies instead. These penalties are mutually exclusive on the same disallowed dollar.

Under 26 U.S.C. § 6664(c)(1), no penalty shall be imposed under IRC § 6662 or § 6663 with respect to any portion of an underpayment if it is shown that there was a reasonable cause for such portion and that the taxpayer acted in good faith with respect to such portion (except for noneconomic substance transactions under § 6662(b)(6) or syndicated conservation easement deductions under § 6662(b)(10)). Similarly, under 26 U.S.C. § 6662(d)(2)(B), the amount of an understatement for purposes of the substantial understatement penalty is reduced by any portion attributable to: (i) the tax treatment of any item for which there is or was "substantial authority," or (ii) any item where the relevant facts affecting its tax treatment are adequately disclosed in the return (or an attached statement) and there is a "reasonable basis" for the tax treatment (unless the item is attributable to a tax shelter under § 6662(d)(2)(C), defined as a partnership, entity, plan, or arrangement having a significant purpose of avoiding or evading federal income tax). However, under 26 U.S.C. § 6664(d)(4)(B) (and parallel reasonable-cause standards), a taxpayer cannot establish reasonable belief by relying on a "disqualified tax advisor"—including an advisor who has a fee arrangement contingent on all or part of the intended tax benefits being sustained (§ 6664(d)(4)(B)(ii)(III))—or on a "disqualified opinion" that is based on unreasonable factual or legal assumptions, unreasonably relies on representations of the taxpayer or others, or fails to identify and consider all relevant facts (§ 6664(d)(4)(B)(iii)).

The 20% penalty rate applies to negligence or disregard of rules or regulations and substantial understatement of income tax under 26 U.S.C. § 6662(a) and (b)(1)–(2), as well as to erroneous refund or credit claims under 26 U.S.C. § 6676(a). A 40% penalty rate applies under 26 U.S.C. § 6662(h) to gross valuation misstatements and under § 6662(i) to nondisclosed noneconomic substance transactions. The 75% penalty rate applies exclusively under 26 U.S.C. § 6663(a) (Imposition of fraud penalty, added by Pub. L. 101-239, § 7721(a), Dec. 19, 1989, and in force through November 3, 2026) when any part of any underpayment of tax required to be shown on a return is due to fraud. Under 26 U.S.C. § 6663(b), if the Secretary establishes that any portion of an underpayment is attributable to fraud, the entire underpayment is treated as attributable to fraud, except with respect to any portion that the taxpayer establishes by a preponderance of the evidence is not attributable to fraud. Negligence under IRC § 6662(c) never carries a 50% or 75% statutory penalty rate.
2.3 Operational Rework, Audit Defense Costs, and Multi-Year Examination Exposure

When the IRS selects an R&D tax credit claim for examination or issues an initial disallowance, the claiming organization incurs substantial direct and indirect operational costs. As documented in the IRS Audit Techniques Guide: Credit for Increasing Research Activities (i.e. Research Tax Credit) IRC § 41 and the American Institute of CPAs (AICPA) journal The Tax Adviser ("Defending R&D Credits"), the IRS Large Business and International (LB&I, formerly LMSB) division has historically managed R&D credit claims as a high-priority Tier I compliance issue. IRS examiners initiate R&D audits by issuing Information Document Requests (IDRs) demanding complete project lists, business-component mappings, internal budgeting documentation detailing experimental efforts, product release sign-offs, contracts governing customer funding and intellectual property rights, and underlying project accounting records.

Defending the claim requires securing and reviewing corroborative evidence, compiling project-level and base-period accounting records, physically inspecting operations, and conducting employee interviews across multiple organizational levels. Although The Tax Adviser notes that Treasury withdrew an early proposed regulation that would have mandated strict contemporaneous documentation of technical problems exceeding the common knowledge of skilled professionals, and while courts in cases such as Union Carbide Corp. v. Commissioner and United States v. McFerrin have permitted admissible oral employee testimony and applied the Cohan rule to accept reasonable approximations when qualified research is established, recent judicial decisions place overwhelming weight on written, contemporaneous, activity-level records. Consequently, senior engineers, scientists, and financial officers (including the CFO) must be diverted from revenue-generating innovation to reconstruct project histories, prepare written transcripts or sworn statements, and sit for IRS examination interviews.

Alongside internal staff diversion, defending a complex IRC § 41 audit or appealing a disallowance requires specialized external tax, legal, and engineering representation. Verification of the underlying sources—WebPT (The True Cost of a Denied Claim in Your PT Practice, September 9, 2022) and the Journal of AHIMA (Claims Denials: A Step-by-Step Approach to Resolution, April 25, 2022)—confirms that these figures measure healthcare medical billing claims: reworking or appealing a denied patient insurance claim averages $25 per claim (estimated in 2017, or $30.50 adjusted for inflation in 2022) for medical and physical therapy practices, roughly $118 per claim in a cited 2017 Becker's Hospital Review report (117–181 across cited summaries), and $181 per claim for hospitals (where unresolved denials average $5 million in annual hospital revenue losses, or up to 5% of net patient revenue). While the comparative point holds—that defending an IRS R&D tax examination at $195 to $395 per hour costs orders of magnitude more than reworking a routine administrative medical insurance claim—readers must note that the $25 to $181 figures are healthcare revenue-cycle benchmarks rather than tax administration statistics.

Furthermore, an R&D credit disallowance in a single tax year alerts the IRS to systemic flaws in the taxpayer's cost-accounting or substantiation methodology, frequently prompting examiners to expand the examination across all open prior and subsequent tax years. For example, in Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113, the IRS audited research credits generated across four consecutive research years (2013 through 2016) and disallowed their utilization across five consecutive credit carryforward and examination years (2015 through 2019).

body.text: 2.4 Hypothetical Worked Examples and Real-World Judicial Outcomes of Disallowed R&D Tax Credit Liability
Hypothetical Example 1: Partial Disallowance of an Amended Refund Claim Under IRC § 6676 (Pre-Disbursement)

Following the official calculation methodology in the IRS Practice Unit on IRC § 6676 (PEN-P-006), assume a corporate taxpayer files an amended return (Form 1120-X) claiming a $100,000 R&D tax credit refund, which the IRS freezes for examination prior to issuing a refund check. Following examination, the IRS allows $30,000 of the research credit, disallows $70,000, and determines that the taxpayer lacked reasonable cause for the disallowed portion. Under 26 U.S.C. § 6676(b), the "excessive amount" equals the $100,000 claimed credit minus the $30,000 allowable credit, or $70,000. Under 26 U.S.C. § 6676(a), the 20% erroneous claim penalty equals 20% of $70,000, or $14,000. Because the $70,000 disallowed portion was frozen and never disbursed, no underpayment arises under IRC § 6664(a) and no accuracy-related penalty under IRC § 6662 applies. Instead, the $14,000 penalty under IRC § 6676(a) offsets the $30,000 allowable credit, leaving the taxpayer with a net refund of $16,000 prior to paying external audit defense fees.
Hypothetical Example 2: Full Disallowance of a $100,000 Utilized R&D Credit (Post-Offset Underpayment)

Assume a corporation claims and utilizes a $100,000 R&D tax credit on its original timely filed tax return to reduce its federal income tax paid, and the IRS subsequently disallows 100% ($100,000) of the credit during an examination, resulting in a $100,000 tax underpayment under 26 U.S.C. § 6664(a). The taxpayer must repay $100,000 in principal. In addition, the 20% accuracy-related penalty for negligence or substantial understatement under 26 U.S.C. § 6662(a) and (b)(1)–(2) adds $20,000 (20% of $100,000), bringing principal plus statutory penalty to $120,000 (with no additional 20% penalty under IRC § 6676 due to the anti-stacking coordination rule in 26 U.S.C. § 6676(d)). By contrast, if the underpayment were attributable to a gross valuation misstatement under 26 U.S.C. § 6662(h), the 40% penalty would equal $40,000 ($140,000 principal plus penalty), and if the IRS proved civil tax fraud under 26 U.S.C. § 6663(a), the 75% penalty would equal $75,000 ($175,000 principal plus penalty). If defending the examination requires 100 hours of external specialist representation at the rate of $195 to $395 per hour, professional defense fees add $19,500 to $39,500 (midpoint: $29,500). Combined with the $100,000 principal repayment and the $20,000 IRC § 6662(a) penalty, total outlay reaches $139,500 to $159,500 ($1.40 to $1.60 per $1.00 of disallowed credit) before adding multi-year compounded underpayment interest under IRC § 6601.
Real-World Judicial Outcome: Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113

In Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113, Docket No. 4759-22 (decided December 23, 2024), the taxpayer generated and claimed R&D tax credits across four research years—$138,205 in 2013; $158,031 in 2014; $138,334 in 2015; and $128,228 in 2016—and utilized those credits to offset tax across five examination years from 2015 through 2019 (utilizing $110,576 in 2015; $74,488 in 2016; $211,142 in 2017; $68,147 in 2018; and $71,102 in 2019). Following an IRS examination (Notice of Deficiency issued December 14, 2021) and a Tax Court trial of a nonbinding three-project sample selected from more than 200 projects, the Tax Court sustained the IRS's disallowance in full and upheld accuracy-related penalties under IRC § 6662(a) as stipulated by the parties across all five utilization years. Across the five credit utilization years, the credit denial resulted in $461,741 in assessed tax deficiencies plus $91,806 in IRC § 6662(a) accuracy-related penalties, totaling $553,547 prior to multi-year statutory underpayment interest under IRC § 6601 and trial litigation expenses.

body.text: III. Regulatory and Judicial Drivers of R&D Tax Credit Denials

Contemporary R&D tax credit denials are driven by three converging compliance pressures: strict judicial enforcement of the Four-Part Test under IRC § 41(d)(1), granular business-component reporting mandated by Section G of revised IRS Form 6765, and formal IRS sufficiency screening of amended refund claims.
3.1 Judicial Precedents Enforcing the Four-Part Test: Little Sandy Coal and Phoenix Design Group

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(1)–(2), research activities related to the development or improvement of a business component constitute qualified research only if the taxpayer establishes—separately for each discrete business component (defined in IRC § 41(d)(2)(B) as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention which is to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer) and without falling under the exclusions of IRC § 41(d)(3)(B) or (d)(4)—that the activities satisfy all four statutory tests:

items: The Section 174 Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(A); 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(2)(i), (a)(3)(i); 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1)): Expenditures with respect to the research must be treatable as expenses under IRC § 174. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i), research is undertaken for the purpose of discovering information if it is intended to eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a business component, which exists when the information available to the taxpayer does not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the business component, or the appropriate design of the business component. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii)–(iii), the taxpayer need not seek information that exceeds, expands, or refines the common knowledge of skilled professionals in the field, nor must the research succeed (and issuance of a utility patent under 35 U.S.C. § 151, other than a design patent under 35 U.S.C. § 171, serves as conclusive evidence that technological information eliminating uncertainty was discovered).

The Technological in Nature Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i); 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(4)): The process of experimentation used to discover the information must fundamentally rely on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science (though a taxpayer may employ existing technologies and rely on existing scientific or engineering principles).

The Business Component / Permitted Purpose Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii), (d)(3); 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(2)(ii), (a)(5)(ii)): The application of the discovered information must be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer, and the process of experimentation must relate to a qualified purpose—specifically, a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality of the business component (excluding research related to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors under IRC § 41(d)(3)(B)).

The Process of Experimentation (POE) Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(C); 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i), (a)(6)): "Substantially all" of the research activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation that relates to a qualified purpose. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i), a process of experimentation is an evaluative process designed to evaluate one or more alternatives to achieve a result where the capability, method, or appropriate design is uncertain as of the beginning of the taxpayer's research activities, involving the identification of uncertainty, the identification of one or more alternatives intended to eliminate that uncertainty, and the conduct of a process of evaluating those alternatives (through modeling, simulation, or a systematic trial and error methodology). Crucially, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) stipulates that the mere existence of design uncertainty at the outset does not establish that all activities undertaken to achieve the new or improved business component constitute a process of experimentation. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6), the "substantially all" requirement is satisfied only if 80 percent or more of a taxpayer's research activities for that business component, measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis (and without regard to 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2)), constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose.

body.text: If an overall product or process fails the four-part test at the whole-component level, the "shrinking-back" rule under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2) instructs applying the four tests to the most significant subset of elements of the product or process, stepping down to smaller subcomponents until either a compliant subcomponent is reached or the most basic element of the product or process fails the requirements. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(d) (cross-referencing 26 CFR § 1.6001-1), the taxpayer must retain records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that the expenditures claimed are eligible for the credit at whichever component or subcomponent level is asserted.

Two landmark decisions highlight how failure to document these statutory elements leads to complete credit disallowance. In Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-15, aff'd, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. March 7, 2023), a shipbuilding subsidiary claimed R&D credits for designing and building first-in-class vessels as "pilot models" under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4)—defined as any representation or model of a product produced to evaluate and resolve uncertainty concerning the product during its development or improvement. The Tax Court disallowed the credits, holding that the taxpayer failed to substantiate that at least 80% of its research activities constituted elements of a Process of Experimentation. Notably, in T.C. Memo. 2021-15, the Tax Court excluded production wages, direct supervision, and direct support from the numerator of the 80% "substantially all" fraction. On appeal in 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023)—which carries higher judicial authority than the Tax Court memorandum opinion, as later recognized by the Tax Court itself in Intermountain Electronics, Inc. v. Commissioner (Docket No. 11019-19)—the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit disagreed with the Tax Court's categorical exclusion of production and support activities on pilot models, holding that production activities on a pilot model can be included in the numerator if they are part of an experimental evaluation. Nevertheless, the Seventh Circuit affirmed the 100% credit denial because the taxpayer relied on generalized trial testimony and arbitrary management percentage estimates rather than contemporaneous, activity-level documentation (such as design iterations, test results, and engineering notes) to establish what fraction of employee time was spent on experimentation, precluding both whole-vessel qualification and any application of the shrinking-back rule.

Similarly, in Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113 (Docket No. 4759-22, December 23, 2024), a C-corporation mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and fire protection (MEPF) consulting engineering firm claimed research credits across more than 200 building design projects. Judge Greaves disallowed 100% of the credits across all three trial sample projects—the Gerald Champion Military Psychiatric Unit (Project No. 13008.00), Baptist Memorial Health North Mississippi Oxford (Project No. 13003.00), and the Vanderbilt University Engineering and Science Building (Project No. 12010.01)—and sustained $91,806 in 20% IRC § 6662 accuracy-related penalties. First, the Tax Court held that technical uncertainty under IRC § 174 is an objective test based on information available at the beginning of research, finding that initial architect schematic block diagrams and historical data already provided Phoenix Design Group with the information required to size systems. Second, the Court held that merely complying with building codes or industry standards, performing routine engineering calculations on available data (such as calculating duct size from airflow), or relocating HVAC air handling units to a roof based on client preference rather than experimental testing does not constitute qualified research. Third, the Court rejected the taxpayer's reliance on the standard six-stage American Institute of Architects (AIA) linear design phases as a substitute for an iterative, scientific-method evaluation of alternatives under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C). Finally, because engineers logged hours under generic labels ("design," "mark-ups," "SD," "project coordination") without linking employee time to specific subcomponent experiments, the Court could not apply the shrinking-back rule under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) to discrete mechanical, electrical, or plumbing subsystems, emphasizing that a taxpayer cannot shrink a business component back merely to a design phase or to specific employees.
3.2 Business-Component Granularity Under Revised IRS Form 6765 (Section G)

The IRS has formally embedded these judicial substantiation standards into tax return reporting through the revised Form 6765, Credit for Increasing Research Activities. Under the official IRS Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. January 2025 / December 2025, updated February 6, 2026 and April 30, 2026), Section G (Business Component Information) requires taxpayers to report granular financial and technical data directly on the tax return for at least 80% of total Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) in descending order by total QREs per business component, up to a maximum of 50 business components (the "80%/Top 50" rule, determined at the controlled group level, with any remaining business components reported on a single line labeled "Aggregate Business Components" in Column 49(c)). Members of a controlled group filing separate tax returns must report at least 80% of their individual total QREs across up to 50 business components. Taxpayers electing the ASC 730 Directive by checking "Yes" on Line 41 may report their ASC 730 Directive Appendix B (Column A) amounts as a single line entry labeled "ASC 730 Directive" in Column 49(c) (entered in Columns 53, 54, 55, and 56), which is not counted toward the 50-component limit and satisfies Section G entirely if it comprises at least 80% of total QREs reported on Line 48. Taxpayers utilizing statistical sampling under Rev. Proc. 2011-42 must still report the 80%/Top 50 business components, append the word "sample" to sampled component names in Column 49(c), and attach their sampling plan as a PDF named Form6765StatSamplePlan.pdf. Paper filers with more than 15 business components must attach additional Section G sheets and report the sum on the "Total from Attachments" line.

body.text: Regarding effective dates and small-taxpayer exemptions, the official IRS Instructions for Form 6765 specify that Section G was optional for all filers for tax years beginning before 2026 (unless filing an amended return claiming a research credit) and is mandatory for tax years beginning after 2025 (i.e., 2026 tax years and forward), subject to exemption criteria. In contrast, the official IRS Instructions for Form 6765—which carry controlling administrative authority—establish that a taxpayer is exempt from completing Section G if it either: (a) is a qualified small business (as defined under IRC § 41(h)(3)) that checked the box to claim the reduced payroll tax credit, or (b) has total QREs determined at the controlled group level on Line 48 of $1.5 million or less AND average annual gross receipts for the prior three tax years of $50 million or less (as determined under IRC § 448(c)(3)), AND is reporting the research credit on an original return.
3.3 IRS Refund Claim Screening, the Classifier Claim Correction, and Enforcement Resources
1. Correction Regarding the "Classifier Review System" and Meyer, Borgman & Johnson

In Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2022-127, aff'd, 100 F.4th 986 (8th Cir. 2024), a structural engineering firm claimed approximately $190,000 in R&D tax credits for tax years 2010, 2011, and 2013. Both the Tax Court (on summary judgment) and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit disallowed the credits under the funded-research exclusion of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) because payment under the firm's fixed-price engineering design contracts was contingent on general professional standards of care rather than contingent on the success of research outcomes.

Instead, actual IRS administrative screening of research credit refund claims is governed by Treasury Regulation § 301.6402-2(b)(1), IRS Office of Chief Counsel Memorandum 20214101F, LB&I directive LB&I-04-0125-0001 (updated January 3, 2025, modifying IRM 4.46.3.7.6), and official IRS Amended Return Research Credit FAQs. Under Treas. Reg. § 301.6402-2(b)(1), an administrative claim for refund or credit must set forth in detail each ground upon which a credit or refund is claimed and facts sufficient to apprise the Commissioner of the exact basis thereof, verified by a written declaration signed under penalties of perjury (typically satisfied by signing Form 1040-X or Form 1120-X); meeting this specificity requirement is a jurisdictional prerequisite to maintaining a tax refund suit in federal court under 26 U.S.C. § 7422(a).

Following an initial grace period that ended January 10, 2022, the IRS initially required five items of information at the time an R&D refund claim was filed. Effective for refund claims postmarked on or after June 18, 2024, the IRS waived the requirement to include two of those items—the names of the individuals who performed each research activity (or, under FAQ 10, the specific number and title/position of the individuals) and the specific information each individual sought to discover—at initial intake (though examiners may still request those two items if the claim is selected for substantive audit), requiring three core items of information at filing alongside the signed perjury declaration:

items: Identify Business Components: Identify all the business components (as defined in IRC § 41(d)(2)(B)) that form the factual basis of the Section 41 research credit claim for the claim year.

Describe Research Activities Performed: For each business component, provide descriptions of all research activities performed, including a description of what the taxpayer did and how they did it (while the submission need not detail the four-part test under IRC § 41(d)(1) in full, language that merely restates statutory or regulatory definitions from the Code or Treasury Regulations is insufficient).

Provide Total Qualified Expenses: Provide the total dollar amount of each of the three tangible expense categories for the claim year: (a) total qualified employee wage expenses, (b) total qualified supply expenses, and (c) total qualified contract research expenses (which may be fulfilled by properly completing Form 6765 or its equivalent).

body.text: Under IRM 4.46.3.7.6 and directive LB&I-04-0125-0001, research credit refund claims are screened for these three procedural sufficiency items at IRS campus intake or by Area Planning and Special Programs (PSP) and field examiners within 30 days of receipt. If a timely filed claim under IRC § 6511(a) is determined to be deficient during the IRS transition period—which began January 10, 2022, was extended through January 10, 2026 in LB&I-04-0125-0001, and was subsequently extended twice for an additional four years through January 10, 2027 per official IRS FAQ guidance updated October 1, 2026—the IRS notifies the taxpayer via Letter 6428 (Claim for Credit for Increasing Research Credit Activities - Additional Information Required) or Letter 6426C, detailing which required items are missing and granting the taxpayer 45 days from the letter date to perfect the claim (accompanied by a new signed declaration under penalties of perjury). Only if the taxpayer fails to submit sufficient information within the 45-day perfection window (or files a deficient claim after the transition period expires) does the IRS reject processing of the claim by issuing Letter 6430 (No Consideration, Section 41 Claim), which informs the taxpayer that the deficient claim cannot be considered (an administrative refusal to process rather than a formal substantive claim disallowance). Crucially, under LB&I-04-0125-0001 and IRM 4.46.3.7.6, prior to issuing Letter 6430 to any taxpayer, both IRS Management (specifically the Territory Manager for LB&I cases or the Area PSP Section Chief for Small Business/Self-Employed [SB/SE] cases) and IRS Office of Chief Counsel must formally review and concur that the claim fails to include the three required items. Thus, intake rejection is neither fully automated nor devoid of human and legal oversight.
2. Correction Regarding the "87,000 New IRS Agents" Under the Inflation Reduction Act

Primary legislative verification confirms that Section 10301 of the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (Pub. L. 117-169, enacted August 16, 2022) appropriated approximately $79.6 billion in multi-year supplemental funding through September 30, 2031—comprising roughly $45.6 billion for enforcement (approximately 58% of the total), $25.3 billion for operations support, $4.8 billion for business systems modernization, and $3.18 billion for taxpayer services—and contained no statutory headcount quota of 87,000 agents.

Instead, the "87,000" figure is a rounded reference to 86,852 full-time equivalent (FTE) positions projected over a 10-year horizon (2022–2031) in Table 3 (page 16) of the U.S. Department of the Treasury's May 2021 report, The American Families Plan Tax Compliance Agenda. In that Treasury table, cumulative FTE projections under the Mandatory Component ($72,467 million cost; $265,896 million total direct and protected revenue) rose from 2,642 FTEs in 2022 to 29,783 FTEs in 2026 and 81,743 FTEs in 2031, while the Program Integrity Cap Adjustment Component ($6,700 million cost; $38,633 million in direct revenue and $11,647 million in protected revenue) projected 5,109 FTEs annually from 2023 through 2031, yielding a combined 2031 total of 86,852 FTEs (81,743 + 5,109). That gross projection spanned all IRS personnel categories—customer service representatives, information technology specialists, operations staff, and replacements for roughly 50,000 retiring employees—whereas total IRS Revenue Agents (8,321 FTEs) and Criminal Investigation Special Agents (2,004 FTEs) numbered only 10,325 combined out of 78,661 total IRS FTEs in FY 2021. Furthermore, subsequent legislation—including Section 251 of the Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023 (Pub. L. 118-5)—and 2025 federal workforce reductions documented in the January 2026 public report (IRS Publication 5316) rescinded portions of IRA enforcement funding and reduced the IRS workforce by more than 25% from its 2024 level of roughly 96,000 FTEs. Consequently, heightened IRS scrutiny of corporate R&D tax credit claims in 2026 is driven primarily by automated return-level data analytics, the mandatory business-component granularity of Form 6765 Section G, and strict campus/PSP refund-claim sufficiency screening rather than an influx of 87,000 new revenue agents.
IV. Mitigating R&D Tax Credit Denial Risk Through Specialized Compliance
4.1 Conservative Claim Methodology and Penalty Insulation

From a statutory tax compliance standpoint, operating under a conservative, fixed-fee methodology directly addresses two major penalty triggers under Title 26. First, by proactively filtering out routine engineering calculations, code-compliance design work, post-production expenses, unsubstantiated wage estimates, and customer-funded fixed-price contracts that fail the judicial standards of Little Sandy Coal, Phoenix Design Group, or Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, a conservative advisor reduces the probability that claimed QREs will be disallowed as an "excessive amount" under 26 U.S.C. § 6676(b) or generate a substantial understatement of income tax under 26 U.S.C. § 6662(d). Second, under 26 U.S.C. § 6664(d)(4)(B)(ii)(III) (and parallel reasonable-cause standards), a tax advisor who has a fee arrangement contingent on all or part of the intended tax benefits from the transaction being sustained is statutorily classified as a "disqualified tax advisor" whose opinion cannot be relied upon to establish the taxpayer's reasonable belief. Engaging an independent specialist on an upfront fixed-fee or hourly ($195 to $395 per hour) basis eliminates the contingent-fee conflict of interest that incentivizes aggressive claim inflation.
4.2 Exclusive Specialization, AI Documentation (TaxTrex), and the Six-Eye Review Process

Pairing AI-driven data structuring—capable of mapping component-by-component direct conduct wages (Column 50), direct supervision wages (Column 51), direct support wages (Column 52), supplies (Column 54), computer leasing (Column 55), and contract research expenses (Column 56) required by Form 6765 Section G—with a mandatory three-discipline human review directly targets the dual nature of R&D audit failures. Whereas accounting-only reviews frequently overlook the scientific and engineering thresholds of objective uncertainty and the 80% Process of Experimentation test (Phoenix Design Group and Little Sandy Coal), and engineering-only narratives often misapply IRC § 41(b) wage exclusions or IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) funded-research rules (Meyer, Borgman & Johnson), a combined technical and tax review validates both scientific eligibility and tax accounting accuracy before the return is submitted to the IRS.
4.3 Audit Defense Cost Transfer (creditARMOR) and Comparative Risk Benchmarks

items: Self-Reported Specialist R&D Audit Rates (1.3% to <5%): Specifically, Black Line Group reports in its consultancy publications (September 15, 2020 and November 11, 2020) that specialized R&D tax credit firms with high integrity expect IRS audit rates between 1% and 2%, and that 1.3% of Black Line Group's own R&D clients are audited by the IRS. Black Line Group also identifies four primary IRS audit triggers for R&D claims: (i) the overall dollar size of the credit claimed, (ii) the ratio of the credit claimed compared to the industry average, (iii) filing the R&D credit via an amended prior-year return (which receives heightened IRS scrutiny), and (iv) whether the IRS deems R&D expenses customary in the taxpayer's specific industry. Similarly, Tax Point Advisors self-reports (March 20, 2024 and August 28, 2024) an IRS audit rate of under 5% and a 0% credit loss rate under audit (noting that fewer than 33%, or ~10% per IRS estimates, of eligible companies claim the credit due to fear of audit), attributing its record to pre-completion defense reviews and multi-disciplinary teams of engineers, CPAs, and tax attorneys.
Generalist Denial Rate Estimates (17% to 20%+): No independent IRS statistical release establishes a 17% to 20% denial rate for generalist CPA R&D tax credit filings.

body.text: V. Strategic Conclusions on Preventing R&D Tax Credit Denials

A disallowance triggers 100% principal recapture (or refund freeze and rejection), compounding statutory underpayment interest running from the unextended original return due date under 26 U.S.C. § 6601(a) and (b)(1), a 20% civil penalty under either 26 U.S.C. § 6676(a) (for excessive refund or credit claims) or 26 U.S.C. § 6662(a) (for tax underpayments attributable to negligence or substantial understatement of income tax), and tens of thousands of dollars in external specialist defense fees ($195 to $395 per hour) alongside severe internal engineering distraction.
To insulate against R&D tax credit denial and its compounding liabilities, corporate taxpayers should execute four compliance practices:

items: Substantiate Objective Uncertainty and the 80% Process of Experimentation Contemporaneously: In accordance with Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner (62 F.4th 287) and Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2024-113), document the specific technical capability, method, or design uncertainty at the outset of each project, maintain dated records of hypotheses, modeling, simulation, and iterative trial-and-error testing, and track employee time by specific research activity and subcomponent rather than generic department or linear AIA design phase labels so that both the 80% "substantially all" threshold (26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6)) and the shrinking-back rule (26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2)) can be established upon examination.

Align Cost-Accounting Systems with Form 6765 Section G Granularity: For tax years beginning after 2025 (unless exempt under the qualified small business payroll tax election under IRC § 41(h)(3) or the original-return safe harbor for controlled groups with $1.5 million or less in QREs and $50 million or less in prior three-year average annual gross receipts under IRC § 448(c)(3)), structure project accounting to capture direct conduct wages (Column 50), direct supervision wages (Column 51), direct support wages (Column 52), supplies (Column 54), computer leasing (Column 55), and contract research expenses (Column 56) for each discrete business component comprising at least 80% of total QREs (up to 50 business components).

Satisfy All Three Specificity Requirements on Amended Refund Claims: When claiming an R&D credit refund on an amended return, include the three mandatory items required under Treas. Reg. § 301.6402-2(b)(1) and IRS directive LB&I-04-0125-0001—identifying all business components, describing what research activities were performed and how they were performed for each component without merely repeating statutory language, and reporting total qualified wage, supply, and contract research expenses, accompanied by a signed declaration under penalties of perjury—at initial filing to avoid receiving a Letter 6428 / 6426C deficiency notice (45-day perfection window through January 10, 2027) or a Letter 6430 refusal to consider.

Engage Independent, Conservative Multi-Disciplinary Review and Audit Insurance: Utilizing fixed-fee specialists who combine specialized R&D compliance software (such as TaxTrex and Substantiation Trackers), mandatory multi-disciplinary human review across engineering, science, and tax law (the six-eye review process), and audit defense fee insurance (such as creditARMOR) eliminates contingent-fee advisor disqualifications under 26 U.S.C. § 6664(d)(4)(B) and caps financial exposure in the event of an IRS examination.
